doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Getting a first guitar and learning chords
summary: His brother's friend sold him a two-pound acoustic at fourteen; Perry taught him chords and he describes his bar-chord cheat.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: When did the guitar come into your hands?

Fourteen years old, 1976. My brother got fed up. He bought one the year before and he got fed up with my messing his scratch plate up. He’s one of those people who cares what his guitar looks like. He’s a very good guitarist himself and to sort of keep me off his guitar he prevailed on his best pal to sell me his guitar, which was like basically almost just one step up from a cigar box with a cheese cutter sort of strings on it.
No it was acoustic. Two quid that cost me. I don’t think it even had a brand name you know.
When you first started learning chords, I’m not sure how to put this, but did you know what they were?
Yeah. You mean the names of them?

Yeah Perry, my brother, taught me the first. And the one that really looks as if it’s going to be difficult is an open G and you see someone do it and you think how do you distort your finger? And that’s really easy but it looks difficult. So but the ones that actually drove me to tears were the bar chords. But once I got hold of them, as my wife will tell you I cheat with the A shaped bar chords. You’re supposed to have these three fingers together and then that bar across. See I can’t do that so I just use the little finger and turn
it into a sixth. And if I don’t want it to be a sixth I don’t hit the thinnest string. That’s how I get round it.
It’s funny you mentioned the sixth because one of my favorite songs of yours, which we’ll get to, has sixes all over it.
Is that right. Oh the chords you mean? A lot of them do I think, yeah. But all right, we’ll get to it.
